{{Short description|Concept in theory of differential equations}}
'''LaSalle's invariance principle''' (also known as the '''invariance principle''',<ref name=Khalil>{{cite book|last1=Khalil|first1=Hasan|title=Nonlinear Systems|date=2002|publisher=Prentice Hall|location=Upper Saddle River NJ|edition=3rd}}</ref> '''Barbashin-Krasovskii-LaSalle principle''',<ref name=Haddad>{{cite book|last1=Wassim|first1=Haddad|last2=Chellaboina|first2=VijaySekhar|title=Nonlinear Dynamical Systems and Control, a Lyapunov-based approach|date=2008|publisher=Princeton University Press}}</ref> or '''Krasovskii-LaSalle principle''') is a criterion for the [[asymptotic stability]] of an autonomous (possibly nonlinear) [[dynamical system]].

== Global version ==

Suppose a system is represented as

: <math> \dot{\mathbf{x}} = f \left(\mathbf x \right) </math>

where <math>\mathbf x</math> is the vector of variables, with

: <math> f \left( \mathbf 0 \right) = \mathbf 0. </math>

If a <math>C^1</math>(see [[Smoothness]]) [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>V(\mathbf x)</math> can be found such that

: <math> \dot{V}(\mathbf x) \le 0 </math>  for all <math> \mathbf x</math>  (negative semidefinite),

then the set of [[accumulation point]]s of any trajectory {{Clarify|reason=please define the concept of accumulation point for a trajectory|date=June 2024}} is contained in <math>{\mathcal I}</math> where <math>{\mathcal I}</math> is the union of complete trajectories contained entirely in the set <math> \{\mathbf x : \dot{V}( \mathbf x) = 0 \}</math>. 

If we additionally have that the function <math>V</math> is positive definite, i.e.

: <math>V( \mathbf x) > 0 </math>,   for all  <math> \mathbf x \neq \mathbf 0</math>
: <math> V( \mathbf 0) = 0 </math>

and if <math>{\mathcal I}</math> contains no trajectory of the system except the trivial trajectory <math>\mathbf x(t) = \mathbf 0</math> for <math>t \geq 0</math>, then the origin is [[asymptotic stability|asymptotically stable]].

Furthermore, if <math>V</math> is radially unbounded, i.e.

: <math> V(\mathbf x) \to \infty </math>, as     <math> \Vert \mathbf x \Vert \to \infty </math>

then the origin is globally [[asymptotic stability|asymptotically stable]].

== Local version ==

If 
: <math>V( \mathbf x) > 0 </math>,   when  <math> \mathbf x \neq \mathbf 0</math>
: <math> \dot{V}(\mathbf x) \le 0 </math>

hold only for <math> \mathbf x </math> in some neighborhood <math>D</math> of the origin, and the set

: <math> \{ \dot{V}( \mathbf x) = 0 \} \cap D </math>

does not contain any trajectories of the system besides the trajectory <math>\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf 0, t \geq 0</math>, then the local version of the invariance principle states that the origin is locally [[asymptotic stability|asymptotically stable]].

== Relation to Lyapunov theory ==

If <math> \dot{V} ( \mathbf x) </math> is negative definite, then the global asymptotic stability of the origin is a consequence of [[Lyapunov stability|Lyapunov's second theorem]]. The invariance principle gives a criterion for asymptotic stability in the case when <math>\dot{V}(\mathbf x)</math> is only negative semidefinite.

== Examples ==
[[File:LaSalle principle example.png|thumb|A plot of vector field <math>(\dot x, \dot y) = (-y-x^3, x^5)</math> and Lyapunov function <math>V(x, y) = x^6 + 3y^2</math>.]]

=== Simple example ===
Example taken from ''"LaSalle's Invariance Principle, Lecture 23, Math 634", by Christopher Grant''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grant |first=Christopher |date=1999-10-22 |title=LaSalle's Invariance Principle, Lecture 23, Math 634 |url=http://www.math.byu.edu/~grant/courses/m634/f99/lec23.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190714024047/http://www.math.byu.edu/~grant/courses/m634/f99/lec23.pdf |archive-date=2019-07-14  |access-date=2022-06-28 }}</ref>

Consider the vector field <math>(\dot x, \dot y) = (-y-x^3, x^5)</math> in the plane. The function <math>V(x, y) = x^6 + 3y^2</math> satisfies <math>\dot V = -6x^8</math>, and is radially unbounded, showing that the origin is globally asymptotically stable.

=== Pendulum with friction ===
This section will apply the invariance principle to establish the local [[asymptotic stability]] of a simple system, the pendulum with friction. This system can be modeled with the differential equation<ref name="ee580">[http://www.nd.edu/~lemmon/courses/ee580/ Lecture notes on nonlinear control], University of Notre Dame,  Instructor: Michael Lemmon, lecture 4. </ref>

:<math> m l \ddot{\theta} = - m g \sin \theta - k l \dot{\theta} </math>

where <math>\theta</math> is the angle the pendulum makes with the vertical normal, <math>m</math> is the mass of the pendulum, <math>l</math> is the length of the pendulum,  <math>k</math> is the [[friction coefficient]], and [[standard gravity|''g'']] is acceleration due to gravity.

This, in turn, can be written as the system of equations

:<math> \dot{x}_1 = x_2 </math>

:<math> \dot{x}_2 = -\frac{g}{l} \sin x_1 - \frac{k}{m} x_2 </math>

Using the invariance principle, it can be shown that all trajectories that begin in a ball of certain size around the origin <math>x_1 = x_2 = 0</math> asymptotically converge to the origin. We define <math>V(x_1,x_2)</math> as

:<math> V(x_1,x_2) = \frac{g}{l} (1 - \cos x_1) + \frac{1}{2} x_2^2 </math>

This <math>V(x_1,x_2)</math> is simply the scaled energy of the system.<ref name="ee580"/> Clearly, <math>V(x_1,x_2) </math> is [[positive definite]] in an open ball of radius <math>\pi</math> around the origin. Computing the derivative,

:<math> \dot{V}(x_1,x_2) = \frac{g}{l} \sin x_1 \dot{x}_1 + x_2 \dot{x}_2 =  - \frac{k}{m} x_2^2 </math>

Observe that <math>V(0) = 0</math> and <math>\dot{V}(0) = 0</math>. If it were true that <math> \dot{V} < 0 </math>, we could conclude that every trajectory approaches the origin by [[Lyapunov stability|Lyapunov's second theorem]]. Unfortunately, <math> \dot{V} \leq 0 </math> and <math>\dot{V}</math> is only [[negative semidefinite]] since <math>x_1</math> can be non-zero when <math>\dot{V}=0</math>. However, the set

:<math> S = \{ (x_1,x_2) | \dot{V}(x_1,x_2) = 0 \} </math>

which is simply the set

:<math> S = \{ (x_1,x_2) | x_2 = 0 \} </math>

does not contain any trajectory of the system, except the trivial trajectory <math>x =0</math>. Indeed, if at some time <math>t</math>, <math>x_2(t)=0</math>, then because 
<math>x_1</math> must be less than <math>\pi</math> away from the origin, <math> \sin x_1 \neq 0 </math> and <math>\dot{x}_2(t) \neq 0 </math>. As a result, the trajectory will not stay in the set <math>S</math>.

All the conditions of the local version of the invariance principle are satisfied, and we can conclude that every trajectory that begins in some neighborhood of the origin will converge to the origin as <math>t \rightarrow \infty </math>.<ref>[http://cc.ee.ntu.edu.tw/~fengli/Teaching/NonlinearSystems/ Lecture notes on nonlinear analysis], National Taiwan University, Instructor: Feng-Li Lian, lecture 4-2.</ref>

== History ==
The general result was independently discovered by [[Joseph P. LaSalle|J.P. LaSalle]] (then at [[Research Institute for Advanced Studies|RIAS]]) and [[Nikolai Nikolaevich Krasovsky|N.N. Krasovskii]], who published in 1960 and 1959 respectively. While [[Joseph P. LaSalle|LaSalle]] was the first author in the West to publish the general theorem in 1960, a special case of the theorem was communicated in 1952 by Barbashin and [[Nikolai Nikolaevich Krasovsky|Krasovskii]], followed by a publication of the general result in 1959 by [[Nikolai Nikolaevich Krasovsky|Krasovskii]].<ref>Vidyasagar, M. ''Nonlinear Systems Analysis,'' SIAM Classics in Applied Mathematics, SIAM Press, 2002.</ref>
